content: The guidelines for the diagnosis, prevention, and management of cryptococcal disease in HIV-infected individuals, including adults, adolescents, and children, were developed as a supplement to the 2016 consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection. These guidelines were published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in March 2018. Cryptococcal disease is a serious opportunistic infection that primarily affects individuals with advanced HIV disease. It is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in this population. The most common clinical manifestation of cryptococcal disease is cryptococcal meningitis, which accounts for approximately 15% of all AIDS-related deaths globally. The majority of these deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa. In 2014, an estimated 223,100 cases of cryptococcal meningitis resulted in 181,100 deaths among people living with HIV. Less common presentations of cryptococcal disease include pulmonary disease and involvement of the skin, lymph nodes, and bones. Cryptococcal disease is much less common in children with HIV, even in regions with a high burden of the disease among adults. The guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations and good practice guidance on the following aspects of cryptococcal disease management: 1. Diagnosis of Cryptococcal Meningitis: Recommendations are provided on the optimal diagnostic approaches, including the use of cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) testing in serum, plasma, or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). A positive CSF antigen test is indicative of cryptococcal meningitis. 2. Prevention of Invasive Cryptococcal Disease: Strategies include CrAg screening in individuals with advanced HIV disease and pre-emptive fluconazole therapy for those who test positive for CrAg but do not yet have symptoms of meningitis. 3. Treatment of Cryptococcal Meningitis: The guidelines recommend combination antifungal therapy regimens, emphasizing the use of amphotericin B and flucytosine as the preferred induction therapy. Alternative regimens are also discussed for settings where these drugs are not available. 4. Management of Amphotericin B Toxicity: Recommendations are provided for preventing, monitoring, and managing the toxic effects of amphotericin B, including nephrotoxicity and electrolyte imbalances. 5. Adjunctive Therapy: The guidelines recommend against the use of systemic corticosteroids as adjunctive therapy in the treatment of cryptococcal meningitis due to the lack of evidence supporting their benefit and potential for harm. 6. Timing of Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) Initiation: Recommendations are provided on the appropriate timing of ART initiation in individuals with cryptococcal meningitis to balance the risks of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) and the benefits of early ART. The recommendations in these guidelines were developed through a series of meetings of the Guideline Development Group, informed by systematic reviews of the evidence. The guidelines aim to improve outcomes for individuals with cryptococcal disease by providing clear, evidence-based recommendations for healthcare providers.
